hints: Focus on what actually sets the pH here, it is not the oxide itself but the hydroxide formed in water in a saturated solution.
Recall how the solubility of Group 2 hydroxides changes as you go down the group from Mg to Ba.
Link higher solubility to higher concentration of dissolved hydroxide ions, and so to higher pH, to pick the most soluble member.
walkthrough:
**See what forms in water**

Each oxide first reacts with water to make its hydroxide. This hydroxide is what makes the solution alkaline.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{MO(s) + H}_2\text{O(l)} \rightarrow \text{M(OH)}_2\text{(aq)}$$

**Remember what saturated means**

Saturated means no more solid can dissolve. So the pH depends on how much hydroxide can dissolve before the solution is saturated.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{M(OH)}_2\text{(s)} \rightleftharpoons \text{M}^{2+}\text{(aq) + 2OH}^-\text{(aq)}$$

**Apply the Group 2 solubility trend**

Solubility of Group 2 hydroxides increases down the group. Magnesium hydroxide is very sparingly soluble, while barium hydroxide is much more soluble.

Chemical equation or calculation rule if applicable:
$$\text{Solubility: Mg(OH)}_2 < \text{Ca(OH)}_2 < \text{Sr(OH)}_2 < \text{Ba(OH)}_2$$

**Connect solubility to pH**

More dissolved $\text{OH}^-$ means higher $\text{[OH}^-\text{]}$ and therefore higher pH. So the most soluble hydroxide, from BaO, gives the saturated solution with the highest pH.

options.A: Correct. BaO forms $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$, which is the most soluble of the four hydroxides. In a saturated solution it gives the highest concentration of $\text{OH}^-$ ions, so the highest pH.
options.B: Not correct. CaO forms $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$, which is more soluble than $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ but much less soluble than $\text{Ba(OH)}_2$ and $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$. Students sometimes pick it because limewater is a familiar alkali, but it does not give the highest pH.
options.C: Not correct. MgO forms $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$, which is the least soluble hydroxide in this list. It gives a very low $\text{[OH}^-\text{]}$ in a saturated solution, so the lowest pH. It is a trap if you think all Group 2 oxides give equally strong solutions.
options.D: Not correct. SrO forms $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$, which is quite soluble and gives a high pH, second only to barium. It is tempting because strontium is just above barium, but the trend continues to increase to barium.
